WARNING — EXCERPT MISATTRIBUTED. The above on-file excerpt does NOT appear in the canonical Millennial Star 40:771-74 document. The Pratt/Smith joint report opens "At Richmond we put up at the Shaw House..." and closes "This ended our interview with the last remaining witness who saw the plates of the Book of Mormon..." — neither "Los Angeles" nor "Sunday School" appears anywhere in the published report. The excerpt is anachronistic for 1878 (Joseph F. Smith's known Los Angeles visits were post-1900). The excerpt almost certainly belongs to a different (later JFS) document and was incorrectly tied to this row in the source CSV. See Provenance for details.

history.citation: St. Louis Republican interview, mid-July 1884, Richmond, Missouri, St. Louis Republican (Missouri Republican), 16 July 1884, p. ?, headlined 'Revelation Revisers.'
history.teaser:
Interest has been revived in questions relating to the origin of the Church of the Latter Day Saints and the authenticity of the manuscript from which the Book of Mormon was printed, and which is now being compared with the various editions of that book by a commission now sitting at Richmond, Mo. ... It has been known for many years that the original manuscript, as dictated by Joseph Smith, and from which the first, or Palmyra (N.Y.) edition of 1830 was printed, has been in possession of David Whitmer of Richmond, who was one of the original, and only surviving witness of the revelator's work.

Whitmer's own statement (verbatim, mid-article):

"Yes, I have no objection to giving the particulars of my early life. I was born near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, at a small trading post, in 1805. My father moved to York state when I was four years old. We settled in Fayette township, Seneca county ... The first time I saw Joseph Smith was in Harmony, Pennsylvania. I joined him before the Book of Mormon was printed at Palmyra, N.Y. I was there during the time the book was printed. The translation was done in my father's house; at least two months of the time, was thus taken up with it there. Oliver Cowdery was the principal amanuensis. ... I saw the stone which formed the box or receptacle in which the metallic plates were found, on the hillside, Commarah. Joseph Smith claimed that an angel informed him of the place where the plates were hidden. I saw the plates; they were bound together with leaves, and held together by rings, two at each corner of the bundle and one in the centre.

"Joseph Smith dictated every word in the book. The understanding we have about it was that when the book was discovered an angel was present and pointed the place out. In translating from the plates, Joseph Smith looked through the Urim and Thumminim, consisting of two transparent pebbles set in the rim of a bow, fastened to a breastplate. He dictated by looking through them to his scribes."

On the seer-stone / "glasses":

"The way that Smith got into the belief of his supernatural power was first by putting on the glasses, he saw his entire past history revealed to him."

On polygamy and the breach with Joseph Smith:

"[Joseph Smith] never to my knowledge advocated it, though I have heard that he virtually sanctioned it at Nauvoo. However, I broke loose from him in 1837 and can't state intelligently."

history.teaser: David Whitmer, one of Richmond's oldest and best known citizens, died at his home Wednesday evening at 6 o'clock, surrounded by his entire family. The Conservator recounts his birth in Harrisburg, Penn. (7 January 1805), his marriage to Julia Ann Jolly (9 January 1831), his moves through Kirtland, Jackson county, Far West, and Richmond (1838), his withdrawal from the Mormon church in 1838 over polygamy, his lifelong testimony as one of the Three Witnesses, and his deathbed declarations to Dr. George W. Buchanan and family ("the Bible and the record of the Nephites … are true").
